great commandments in today’s celebration: we are called to love god and our neighbour: friend, visitor and stranger alike. penitential rite let us call to mind times we have failed to show love, remembering that god never fails to love and forgive us i confess … prayer your love, o god, is boundless. we who were strangers have been made your children. we who were defenceless have been brought into your household. keep us mindful of your deeds of mercy, that we may love you with our whole heart and love our neighbour as ourselves. we ask this through our lord jesus christ, your son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the holy spirit, god for ever and ever. introduction to the scripture readings 1st reading the people of israel are re-minded that in bad times they depended on the kindness of strangers. they should there-fore treat the weak and helpless with com-passion. 2nd. reading paul praises the people of salonika for their good christian living, which they had learned from him. the gospel jesus discloses the greatest commandment — love of god and neigh- bour. seeing your life though the lens of the gospel mt 22:34-40 1. you may feel some sympathy with the jews struggling to cope with 613 laws and wondering which were the important ones. have you ever felt overwhelmed by the rules and regulations of your own tradition? and have you ever been blessed by meeting someone, or reading something, that was able to cut through all the layers and point out to you what is essential in life? who was that person? what dids/he say or do? is there some phrase or text that encapsulates such wisdom for you? 2. if you were asked what is most important in life, what would your answer be? recall the experiences and relationships you have had. which are the ones that you treasure most? what has particularly enriched your life? how would you encourage another person who asked you hows/he could live a full life? 3. in the unusual circumstances of recent years social life was disrupted by covid. we had to find unusual and creative ways of showing love to our neighbours. what ways of reaching out to others did you find were most appreciated? to receive holy communion in the hand, make a "throne" with your hands by placing your non-dominant hand flat on top of your dominant hand, step up to the minister , as he /she says the “body of christ ” respond saying amen, step to the side, con-sume the host immediately in front of the altar making a sign of the cross + before turning to walk away. vocations this month over different themes we pray for reflection: the saints as stained glass windows i think of the saints as stained- glass windows. an ordinary window lets in the sunlight but the stained-glass window gives colour, shape and story to the light. the saints in their various ways show us how to live the christian life. the saints manifest the holy side of the church. they give shape, story and colour to the light of god. they inspire us by their holy lives, instruct us by the ir teaching and give us their protection in answer to our prayers. saint therese of lisieux promised, “i want to spend my heaven doing good on earth.” this november let us recall the light of our beautiful saints that are publicly venerated and especially those we have personally known and loved . see on you tube bravery under fire tells the story of fr willie doyle sj the heroic irish priest & world war 0ne army chaplain who died saving soldiers i know a lot of saints, i do! so let me mention just a few: i know someone who runs a team and teaches kids to play and dream, who stands in cold and wind and rain on days they play and nights they train; someone who’s there when we are sad the best the gentlest friend we’ve had , someone who says, ‘just do your best’, when i am scared to take atest; a friend who takes the time to show how things were done so ; a teacher who just always knows where that comma always goes; and others who are kind and good, who try to act as jesus would, who show god’s love in all they do. i know a lot of saints, don’t you? ( by christy kenneally) one of the most striking aspects of all saints’ day is its universality. unli ke feasts dedicated to specific saints, this day commemorates all the holy men and women who have faithfully followed christ, even if their names and deeds are lost to history. at its heart, all saints’ day is an expression of hope. it points to the transformative power of god’s grace, which turns ordinary people into extraordinary witnesses of love, charity, and faith. the saints, in all their diversity, provide us with a glimpse of what it means to in communion with god. it reminds us that sainthood is not limited to a select few who achieved great or accomplished extraordinary feats; rather, it encompasses countless individuals whose lives, while perhaps quiet or humble, were nonetheless deeply rooted in fait h. these are the mothers and fathers, the workers and neighbours, the ordinary people who lived out thei r discipleship in simple yet profound ways. this day calls us to remembe r that holiness is not reserved for the few but is open to all of us. in the beatitudes which ar read on all saints’ day jesus lays out the path to holiness in a way that is both universal and personal. blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the peacemakers, and those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. these words reveal that sainthood is less about perfection & more about a life oriented toward god & others. the saints are models for us, not because they were sinless, but because they allowed god’s grace to work in and through them, even in their weakness prayer on lighting a candle during november: as you hold this candle in your hand, recall the memory of your loved one. pray god’s peace and rest on their soul. pray also for yourself that god in his infinite love for you will give you peace of mind and heart at this time of brokenness and loss in your life. may the souls of all the faithful depa rted rest in peace. o sacred heart of jesus grant them a place of peace and joy in your kingdom . amen god bless. fr. gearóid walsh, ballybunion

a message from fr timothy: my dear parishioners & friends, it is my hope thaty are all fine and doing well. after the short illness and sad loss of my mother, i want to send a message of thanks to you all. although i have been far away from mill town & listry during these past weeks, the parish team have been keeping me updated and telling me about the many people who have been praying for me and my family, asking after us, and passing on their good wishes. i know so many of you have remem bered my mother, teresia, in your prayers and mass intentions and for that i am deeply grateful. hearing all this while being thousands of miles away has been a grea t comfort to me and my family during this difficult time. i will remain in kenya until after my mother's mont h's mind mass and will return on the evening of thursday, 12th november . while it is important for me to spend this time with my family, i very much miss parish life a nd look forward to being back with you all again soon. as we approach the month of november, i ask you to remember my mother, teresia, and especially all our deceased parishioners in your prayers. november is a time when we remember with love and gratitude those who have gone before us and entrust them to god's mercy. be assured that i am r emembering you all and your families in my prayers each day here in kenya. thank you again for your kindness, friendship, and support. i look forward to seeing you all when i return. every blessing, fr. timothy change of time for the milltown annual masses of remembrance 2026 : our annual masses of . wedding congratulations to annette morris, navan and paddy townes, lower feighmane who were married recently. may they be blessed with a long and happy life. transatlantic cable ensemble unesco world heritage nomination: drop-in clinic mon 2nd nov 7-9pm, tue 3rd 3-5pm & valentia island community group meeting 7-9pm at the royal hotel. kerry county council welcomes members of the public to participate in a planning and demystifying world heritage information clinic regarding the nomination of the transatlantic cable ensemble for unesco world heritage designation. next monday nov 2nd is the commemoration of all the faithful departed. mass at 10 am in chapeltown church. mass of remembrance for all who died during the year will be celebrated on sunday nov 15th at 11 30 am in knightstown. if you wish to have a name added to the list please give name to mary (sacristan) as soon as possible. thank you. november - remembering those we love! november has a special place in our hearts. as the evenings grow darker and the years draw towards its close, we find ourselves thinking of those who are no longer with us. all of us have people we miss: a husband or wife, a parent, a brother or sister, a friend or neighbour. we remember their voices, their smiles, the little things they did, and the memories that remain with us. sometimes it is only when we hear a familiar song, visit a favourite place or sit quietly at home that we realise just how much we still miss them. during november, we are invited to remember our dead in a special way. we light candles, visit their graves and pray for them, trusting them to the loving care of god. grief may never completely leave us, but neither does love. the people we have loved remain part of who we are. may this month bring comfort to those who mourn gratitude for the lives we have shared, and hope in the promise that love is stronger than death. valentia

as we celebrate this weekend the feast of all saints, i'd like to share a powerful sermon by the american preacher john piper, entitled don't waste your life. he began by saying, “the really sad thing is that there are hundreds of you in this crowd who don't want your lives to make a difference." he spoke about two elderly women in their eighties, ruby eliason and laura edwards, who had devoted their lives to serving jesus christ among the poor and sick in cameroon. both were tragically killed in an accident while carrying out their mission. piper asked a very interesting question: “was this a tragedy?" his answer was no. these women had given their lives to something that would last for eternity. he contrasted that with an article he had read in reader's digest, entitled start now, retire early. “bob and penny took early retirement five years ago from their jobs in the northeast. he was 59; she was 51. they now live in punta gorda, florida, where they cruise on their 30-foot trawler, play softball and collect shells!" "now that's a tragedy!" imagine in the last chapter of your life, standing before the creator of the universe to give an account of what you did with your life: “here it is, lord, my shell collection! and look at my boat!" it reminded me of the quote attributed to joan of arc: “i know this now. every man gives his life for what he believes. every woman gives her life for what she believes. sometimes people believe in little or nothing, and yet they give their lives to that little or nothing. one life is all we have, and we live it as we believe in living it, and then it's gone. but to surrender what you are and to live without belief is more terrible than dying—even more terrible than dying young." on this feast of all saints, let us realise the truth of the words of st. irenaeus: “the only real tragedy in life is not to become a saint."

. beaufort pioneer centre will hold a rambling house session on saturday nov. 14th at beaufort community hall . doors open at 8 pm. a great evening of music and song. tea and refreshments served. all welcome fossa parish pastoral council and finance committee offer “céad míle fáilte” to all our visitors. we invite you to consider supporting the upkeep of our christ , the prince of peace church and grounds by means of our “ donate a slate” campaign as outlined in the porch. reflection and so the autumn makes itself known to us in many ways; the trees shedding their leaves; the multi-coloured dead leaves that lie on our pathways, the shorter days and the longer evenings, light gives way to shadow and darkness and thus we are reminded, and indeed remember, our loved ones who have died november is a month with its own energy; it instils in us the gift of remembering those who have gone before us; those who are now on sli na firinne (theway of truth) we remember them and honour their memory, we give thanks for them and their legacies they have left us; perhaps the legacy of integrity, simplicity, peace, and above all, their faith; faith in god and their faith in broken humanity; their understanding from the depth of their being. in this month of november let us honour their memory with gratitude and allow their spirits to go free so that we can receive them in abundance. may their generous souls rest in peace final blessing heavenly father, with the saints to inspire and guide us, may we seek after holiness and thus live lives that are worthy of our christian dignity; we ask this through christ our lord. god bless, fr. noel
